How the total was counted: Sum of hard, 10-Q-quantified items as of 2026-09-26: purchase commitments $48.8B + cloud capacity backstops $6.2B + data-center leases not commenced (to be subleased to partners) $13.3B + partner lease/debt guarantees $8.5B + equity investment commitments $5.1B (assumed to include the Anthropic $5B; Anthropic not added separately) = $81.9B. Excluded: Crusoe $0.3B (likely inside the 10-Q figures), the $1.0B Oct public-company investment (already paid), warrant values (stock-settled, contingent), and multi-GW customer deals (revenue, not obligations). Excluding ordinary supply purchase commitments, the customer-support exposures (capacity backstops + leases + guarantees + equity) are ~$33.1B, about 4.7x trailing-12-month FCF of ~$7.1B. These are maximums; none has been paid out yet.
Biggest hidden risk: If OpenAI, Anthropic or the neoclouds it backs slow their GPU purchases, AMD gets hit at once by unsold inventory against $48.8B of supply commitments plus calls on up to ~$28B of lease guarantees and capacity backstops.
Why: On its own books AMD looks safe: $15.8B cash vs $7.1B debt and A-grade ratings. But the 10-Q shows AMD is now propping up its customers: it guarantees $8.5B of partners' data-center leases and loans, has signed $13.3B of data-center leases it plans to pass to partners, promises to buy $6.2B of cloud capacity nobody else rents, and is investing up to $5B in Anthropic. It also pays OpenAI and Meta in its own stock (up to 320M shares) to buy its GPUs, and owes $48.8B to suppliers, mostly by end-2027. Those customer-support items (~$33B) are about 4-5x AMD's yearly free cash flow, which shrank to $554M last quarter as inventory piled up.
What would change my mind: Seeing MI450/Helios revenue convert to strong free cash flow in Q4 2026-Q1 2027 (inventory falling) while the guarantee, lease and capacity-backstop totals shrink rather than grow.

How the total was counted: Sum of hard, quantified non-debt items from the 10-Q commitments table: leases not yet commenced $164.9B + P&E purchase obligations $159.6B + other unconditional purchase obligations $94.8B + other commitments $19.0B = $438.3B, plus the $15.0B contingent Anthropic financing facility = ~$453.3B. Excluded: on-balance-sheet rows of the same table (debt principal+interest $294.3B, operating leases $121.5B, finance leases $18.0B, financing obligations $11.6B; total table $883.6B), already-funded investments (OpenAI $50B, Anthropic $18B), customer commitments to AWS (revenue, not obligations), standby LCs ($21.6B), tax contingencies ($7.3B). Equals ~2.7x TTM operating cash flow ($168.3B), on top of negative TTM FCF.
Biggest hidden risk: If OpenAI or Anthropic slow their spending, a big chunk of the $578B AWS backlog could shrink while Amazon is still locked into ~$325B of equipment purchases and unstarted leases funded with new debt.
Why: Amazon's reported debt has jumped from $66B to $173B this year and its trailing free cash flow is negative $42B, so even the visible books show strain. Off the balance sheet it has another ~$453B of commitments -- unstarted leases, equipment and energy purchase obligations, and a $15B credit line for Anthropic -- about 2.7x a year of operating cash flow. It has also invested $68B into OpenAI and Anthropic, which together promised ~$248B of AWS spending, a textbook vendor-financing loop. Amazon is still highly rated (AA/A1), has $114B of cash and a now-public Anthropic stake worth far more than it paid, so it is not in danger -- but it is relying on bond markets and on two cash-burning AI labs to make the math work.
What would change my mind: A return to positive free cash flow in 2027 with debt flat, or disclosure that OpenAI+Anthropic are a small share of AWS backlog, would lower this to Moderate; a drop in the Anthropic share price or failed/expensive bond deals would push it to High.

How the total was counted: Hard, filed items: purchase commitments $126.8B + other contractual $3.9B + AI XPV backstop $29B (10-Q) + North Star residual value support $43B (8-K) + Anthropic placement $1B = ~$203.8B. Excluded to avoid double counting: the $42B Anthropic convertible-note commitment (funds the same lease rent the backstops protect) and the unconfirmed $30-50B OpenAI financing. Purchase commitments are largely matched by $179.2B of RPO, so the truly 'hidden' layer is the ~$72B of residual value backstops (plus up to $42B convertible notes), concentrated on one sub-investment-grade customer, Anthropic. Backstops are maximums that only bite if Anthropic defaults AND the racks resell below 72.5-85% of the lease balance.
Biggest hidden risk: If Anthropic stumbles and the leased AI racks have lost value, Broadcom could owe tens of billions under its backstops at the same time its biggest customer stops ordering chips.
Why: Broadcom's own books are strong: ~$13.7B of free cash flow a quarter, $24B cash and falling debt from the VMware deal. But to win chip orders it has promised lenders it will cover losses on Anthropic's chip leases, up to ~$29B (June deal) plus ~$43B (October deal), and may lend Anthropic up to $42B more so it can pay its rent. That is roughly $72-114B of exposure to one customer that the bond market rates junk, about 2-3x Broadcom's yearly free cash flow, and it is negotiating a similar setup for OpenAI. S&P already cut its outlook and Broadcom's CDS hit records, so credit markets see it too.
What would change my mind: Anthropic reaching sustained positive cash flow or an investment-grade rating, or Broadcom shrinking backstops as racks are paid down instead of adding an OpenAI-sized one.

How the total was counted: Hard, quantified obligations not on the balance sheet: $47.4B leases not yet commenced + up to $16.9B single-site capped lease + $2.1B construction commitments + ~$4.0B other purchase commitments + $1.9B JV max loss exposure = ~$72.3B. Excludes Nvidia's $6.3B backstop (an asset/support for CoreWeave, not an obligation), Nvidia's $2B equity, OEM financing (already in debt), prepayments (future liabilities), and backlog/customer commitments (revenue, not obligations). Adding on-balance debt ($47.5B) and lease liabilities ($19.3B), total fixed obligations ~$139B vs TTM operating cash flow ~$7.2B (~19x) and equity ~$4B.
Biggest hidden risk: If a top customer (e.g., Microsoft consolidating neoclouds) cuts or delays capacity while credit markets stay shut, CoreWeave is still on the hook for ~$64B of signed, mostly long-dated leases with no cash cushion to cover them.
Why: CoreWeave already owes about $47.5B of debt plus $19B of booked leases, and on top of that has ~$72B of signed obligations that are not on its balance sheet yet (mostly data-center leases starting 2026-2029). That is many times its ~$7B of yearly operating cash flow and ~$4B of equity, and its interest bill alone is bigger than its operating profit. It survives by continuously raising new money - GPU-backed loans, convertibles, share sales and customer prepayments - and lenders mainly trust the contracts of a few giant customers (Microsoft, OpenAI, Meta), one of which (OpenAI) is itself funded partly by Nvidia. Nvidia's $2B stock purchase and $6.3B 'buy unsold capacity' backstop make the loop look safer, but they are small relative to the obligations, and bond and CDS markets (~16% yields, ~1,200bp CDS) are pricing real default risk.
What would change my mind: Several quarters of positive free cash flow plus investment-grade asset loans closing at ~7% with backlog diversifying away from Microsoft/OpenAI/Meta and CDS falling well below 500bp.

How the total was counted: Sum of hard, 10-Q-quantified items: purchase commitments >1yr $802.1B + leases not commenced $130.5B + data-center credit-derivative backstops $48.0B + energy financial guarantees $16.2B + TPU repurchase guarantees $6.6B = $1,003.4B. Excluded to avoid double counting or because not liabilities: Fluidstack/TeraWulf/Cipher backstops (inside the $48.0B), Crux AI $10B backstop commitment (may later appear in credit derivatives), $10B Anthropic private placement (cash outflow post-quarter, not an ongoing obligation), Anthropic $121.3B and Crux $16.8B (these are backlog/receivable-side concentration, not obligations), open POs ($122.3B within the $924.4B). Note most of the $802.1B is ordinary-course supply/energy purchases; the truly contingent 'hidden debt' (backstops + guarantees) is ~$71B, rising to ~$81B with Crux. Off-balance total ~5.6x TTM operating cash flow ($179.6B).
Biggest hidden risk: If Anthropic or the neocloud tenants Google backstops (Fluidstack and crypto-miner landlords) hit a funding wall, Google simultaneously loses a fifth of its cloud backlog, takes write-downs on a ~$140B equity stake, and has to pay out on tens of billions of lease guarantees.
Why: Alphabet still looks rock-solid on its own books (AA+/Aa2, $265B of cash and securities, ~$180B of yearly operating cash flow), but it is now acting as a lender and guarantor to the AI ecosystem. It backstops about $48B of other companies' data-center leases (including former bitcoin miners renting to Fluidstack), guarantees $16B of energy deals and $6.6B of TPU buybacks, and has $130B of data-center leases about to start plus ~$800B of multi-year purchase commitments. Its biggest cloud customer, Anthropic (~$121B of backlog), is partly financed by Alphabet's own equity checks, and the Crux AI JV is a round trip where Google guarantees a venture that buys from Google. Cash flow just turned negative, buybacks stopped and it is selling stock and long bonds at wider spreads, so it is no longer self-funding. Rating is Elevated rather than High because the core ads business throws off huge cash and the contingent pieces (~$71-81B) are under half a year of operating cash flow.
What would change my mind: A return to positive quarterly free cash flow while backstop notional shrinks and Anthropic's share of cloud backlog falls below ~10% would move this to Moderate.

How the total was counted: Sum: non-cancelable commitments $454.52B + leases not yet commenced $355.73B + JV residual value guarantees $41.49B + JV future funding commitments $3.70B = $855.44B. Excluded to avoid double counting: JV lease commitments $18.48B (assumed within uncommenced leases), JV equity $4.73B (already a balance-sheet asset), Hyperion $27.3B (inside the $68.4B JV exposure), named cloud contracts ~$82B (inside the $454.5B), $14.72B contingent cloud purchases (contingent), $25B New Mexico judgment (litigation, under appeal). Off-balance total is ~6.5x annualized Q3 operating cash flow (~$131B) and ~10x debt face value.
Biggest hidden risk: If AI returns disappoint and Meta wants to cut back, the $356B of signed leases and Hyperion-style residual value guarantees mean it can't easily walk away, so the 'flexible' capex is really fixed, debt-like spending.
Why: On paper Meta has only ~$84B of debt and ~$82B of cash, so a balance-sheet scorecard says it's fine. But it has signed ~$356B of data-center/energy leases that haven't started yet, ~$455B of non-cancelable purchase commitments (including big neocloud contracts with CoreWeave, Nebius, Oracle and Google), and guarantees up to $41.5B of residual value on JVs like Hyperion, where Blue Owl and bondholders put up ~$27B that never shows up as Meta debt. That's roughly $855B of obligations versus maybe ~$130B a year of operating cash flow, at a moment when free cash flow is already negative, buybacks are zero, S&P has a negative outlook, and a $25B court penalty is pending. It isn't Severe because ads revenue still grows 26% and Meta can still borrow at AA-level rates, but it's the most structurally off-balance-sheet hyperscaler.
What would change my mind: Seeing Meta return to positive FCF in 2027 while S&P moves back to stable and the uncommenced-lease and JV exposure totals stop growing would drop this to Elevated.

How the total was counted: Sum of hard, quantified non-debt commitments: leases not yet commenced $364.6B (9/30/26) + purchase commitments $194.1B (6/30/26) + construction commitments $34.6B (6/30/26) + remaining OpenAI funding commitment $1.0B = ~$594.2B. Neocloud contracts (~$70.9B Nscale/Nebius/IREN) are excluded as they are very likely inside purchase commitments. OpenAI RPO share, the $250B Azure commitment, receivables, the IRS claim, and the unconfirmed backstop are exposures/contingencies, not added. Dates are mixed (10-Q does not refresh purchase commitments). For scale: ~3.2x FY2026 operating cash flow (~$183B = FCF $67.0B + capex $115.9B) and ~17x reported debt of $35.5B.
Biggest hidden risk: If OpenAI cannot raise the money to honor its ~$250B Azure commitment, Microsoft is left with hundreds of billions in non-cancelable leases and GPUs built for a customer that isn't paying.
Why: On its own books Microsoft looks nearly debt-free ($35.5B of debt vs $64.5B of cash), which is why a balance-sheet scorer rates it a fortress. But it has signed roughly $365B of datacenter leases that haven't started yet plus ~$230B of purchase and construction commitments -- about 3x a year of operating cash flow. A big chunk of its $677B backlog (45% at end-2025, maybe ~a third now) comes from OpenAI, a money-losing customer that Microsoft helped fund. Microsoft still generates strong positive free cash flow and has AAA ratings, so it can absorb a lot, but the cushion is shrinking as it now borrows to build.
What would change my mind: A disclosed, sharply lower OpenAI share of RPO (diversified backlog) together with capex coming back under operating cash flow would push this to Moderate; OpenAI funding trouble or lease commitments rising past ~$450B would push it to High.

How the total was counted: Hard, quantified off-balance obligations: leases not commenced $13.86B + energy take-or-pay $2.73B + post-quarter Citi facility $3.5B = $20.1B. Compare to ~$14.2B on-balance debt, $7.4B cash and negative Q3 FCF of ~$7.6B. Excluded: customer contracts (they are revenue, not obligations), prepayments (already on balance sheet as deferred revenue), Nvidia equity (already funded), and the ~$6-11B unfunded 2027 capex gap (a forecast, not a contract).
Biggest hidden risk: If third-party data center delays continue, Microsoft could terminate tranches and demand penalties while Nebius is still on the hook for $13.9B of leases and needs to refinance a 364-day bridge in a closed high-yield market.
Why: Nebius plans to spend $40-45B next year while it has $7.4B of cash, burned about $7.6B of free cash flow last quarter, and already owes about $14B (plus a $3.5B one-year Citi bridge). It has also signed about $14B of data center leases that have not started yet and $2.7B of fixed power contracts that are not on the balance sheet as debt. Its plan only works if Microsoft and Meta keep prepaying and lenders keep lending against those contracts, and about 70% of revenue comes from three customers. The bond market is already pulling back (it shelved a junk bond and its converts trade around 70 cents), and its supplier-investor Nvidia is in turmoil. The saving grace is that its biggest customers are investment-grade and prepay a lot.
What would change my mind: Delivery of the remaining Microsoft capacity on the new schedule plus a long-dated, investment-grade asset-backed financing of the Meta/Microsoft contracts that covers 2027 capex without more bridge loans would move me to Elevated.

How the total was counted: Sum of Nvidia's own three disclosed tables at 2026-10-25: $518B commitments (supply $390B + cloud services $28B + leases not commenced $74B + equity investment commitments $20B + capex $6B) + $32B conditional neocloud agreements + $118B maximum guarantees = $668B (~12.5x the $53.5B cash/debt securities). Not added: CoreWeave $6.3B (inside cloud services), Nscale lease guarantee (inside $3.5B), Anthropic/Nscale tranches (likely inside $20B equity commitments), funded investments like OpenAI $30B (already on balance sheet), and receivables. Most of the $390B supply line is normal-course inventory buying; the customer-support portion (neocloud $32B + guarantees $118B + cloud services $28B) is ~$178B, about 1x annualized operating cash flow and ~67% of equity.
Biggest hidden risk: A funding squeeze at OpenAI or the neoclouds would hit Nvidia three ways at once: lost revenue, writedowns on its ~$110B equity portfolio, and guarantee/capacity buy-back payments.
Why: On its own books Nvidia is a fortress: about $32B of debt against $53.5B of cash and debt securities and roughly $48B of operating cash flow per quarter. But off the balance sheet it has signed up for about $668B of commitments and guarantees, including a $105B guarantee that pays only if OpenAI stops paying rent on an Ohio campus. It also owns roughly $110B of stock in AI companies and neoclouds, many of which use outside money (and Nvidia's money) to buy Nvidia chips, and it is giving big buyers longer to pay (receivables doubled to $81B). If AI credit tightens, these customers buy less, the stakes lose value, and the guarantees and buy-back deals start costing real cash all at once.
What would change my mind: If the guarantees and neocloud commitments shrank (as new management hinted) while customer concentration fell and receivables/DSO normalized, I would drop the rating to Moderate.

How the total was counted: Sum of hard, contractually quantified off-balance items only: $288B leases not yet commenced + $34.15B unconditional purchase obligations. Excludes the ~$300B OpenAI contract and $664B RPO (these are revenue/concentration exposures, not obligations), the ~$16B prepayment liability (already on balance sheet), and undisclosed vendor financing. Lease figure is undiscounted and spread over 15-19 years, so it is not comparable to debt one-for-one. For scale: ~$322B vs TTM operating cash flow ~$47B (~7x) and FY2026 OCF $32B (~10x).
Biggest hidden risk: If OpenAI cannot pay or delays its ramp, Oracle is still locked into ~$288B of 15-19-year leases plus vendor-financed hardware for capacity built specifically for OpenAI.
Why: On paper Oracle has ~$125-135B of debt, but it has also signed $288B of data-center leases that are not on the balance sheet yet and $34B of purchase commitments - together roughly 7x a year of operating cash flow. Much of that capacity is being built for one customer, OpenAI, whose ~$300B contract is roughly 45% of Oracle's backlog and who itself depends on outside funding (including from Nvidia). Oracle is also using supplier credit and customer prepayments to keep reported debt and capex down, and it has not said how big the vendor financing is. It is not 'Severe' because Oracle still has a large, profitable software business, investment-grade ratings, and positive operating cash flow - but credit markets (CDS ~300bp+, 7-8.65% new bond coupons) are already pricing it close to junk.
What would change my mind: Evidence that OpenAI's share of RPO is falling fast with diversified new customers, plus Oracle reaching positive FCF on schedule in 2H FY2028 without new debt or a rating cut.
